subject: bio
title: Biological Molecules
subtitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, water and inorganic ions.
concept: Biological molecules are built from monomers joined by condensation reactions; they are broken down by hydrolysis.
Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; their 3D shape is determined by their sequence and determines their function.
Water's unique properties (cohesion, high specific heat capacity, solvent ability) make it essential for life.

notes.heading: Carbohydrates
items: Monosaccharides: hexoses (glucose, fructose, galactose) and pentoses (ribose, deoxyribose). α-glucose has OH on C1 pointing down; β-glucose points up.
Disaccharides: maltose (α-glucose + α-glucose, 1,4-glycosidic), sucrose (α-glucose + fructose), lactose (glucose + galactose).

Polysaccharides: starch (amylose — α1,4; amylopectin — α1,4 and α1,6 branching); glycogen (highly branched, α1,4 and α1,6); cellulose (β1,4 — alternating glucose units, H-bonds between chains give strength).

notes.heading: Lipids
items: Triglyceride: glycerol + 3 fatty acids joined by ester bonds (condensation). Saturated: no C=C double bonds; unsaturated: one or more C=C.
Phospholipid: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate group. Amphipathic — hydrophilic head (phosphate), hydrophobic tails (fatty acid chains); forms bilayer in cell membranes.

notes.heading: Proteins
items: Amino acids linked by peptide bonds (condensation between –NH₂ and –COOH; water released).

Primary: amino acid sequence. Secondary: α-helix or β-pleated sheet (H-bonds). Tertiary: 3D shape (H-bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds, hydrophobic interactions). Quaternary: two or more polypeptide chains.

Fibrous proteins (e.g. collagen, keratin): structural, insoluble, regular repeated sequence. Globular proteins (e.g. enzymes, haemoglobin): functional, soluble, irregular sequence folded into compact shape.

notes.heading: Water
items: Polar molecule (δ+ H, δ− O); forms hydrogen bonds. Cohesion: water molecules stick to each other (surface tension, transpiration stream). High specific heat capacity: resists temperature change. Solvent: dissolves ions and polar molecules. Latent heat of vaporisation: evaporation cools surfaces.

definitions.body: A reaction that joins two monomers, releasing a water molecule.
The bond formed between the –NH₂ group of one amino acid and the –COOH group of another, releasing water.
Irreversible change in the 3D shape of a protein due to disruption of bonds maintaining tertiary structure; the primary structure remains intact.
A sugar that can donate electrons to (reduce) an oxidising agent; includes all monosaccharides and some disaccharides (e.g. maltose, lactose); detected by Benedict's test (brick-red precipitate).

workedExamples.q: Explain why cellulose is suitable for forming plant cell walls.

steps.text: Cellulose is a polysaccharide of β-glucose molecules linked by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds. The alternating orientation of β-glucose units allows straight, unbranched chains.
Hydrogen bonds form between parallel chains, cross-linking them into microfibrils.
The high tensile strength of these microfibrils provides structural support and prevents cells from bursting (cell lysis) under osmotic pressure.

mistakes: Confusing α-glucose (OH down at C1) and β-glucose (OH up at C1).
Stating denaturation 'breaks the primary structure' — primary structure (peptide bonds) is unaffected; denaturation disrupts tertiary/secondary bonds.
Confusing condensation (joins monomers, releases H₂O) with hydrolysis (breaks polymers, uses H₂O).
tips: Learn the Benedict's test: reducing sugar → brick-red; non-reducing sugar (sucrose) → test with HCl first to hydrolyse, then retest.
Iodine/KI solution: starch → blue-black. Biuret reagent: protein → purple.
Emulsion test for lipids: dissolve in ethanol, add water → white emulsion.

flashcards.q: What bond joins amino acids together?
flashcards.a: Peptide bond (formed by condensation between –NH₂ and –COOH groups).

flashcards.q: What is the difference between α-glucose and β-glucose?
flashcards.a: α-glucose has the –OH group on C1 pointing downward; β-glucose has it pointing upward.

flashcards.q: What bonds stabilise the tertiary structure of a protein?
flashcards.a: Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds (between cysteine residues), and hydrophobic interactions.

flashcards.q: What is the reagent for testing for starch, and what is a positive result?

flashcards.a: Glycerol + 3 fatty acids joined by 3 ester bonds via condensation reactions, releasing 3 water molecules.

flashcards.q: Why is water a good solvent?
flashcards.a: Water is polar — the δ+ and δ− regions attract and surround ions and polar molecules, dispersing them in solution.

questions.q: What type of bond joins glucose monomers in cellulose?
questions.exp: Cellulose is formed by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds between β-glucose monomers.

questions.q: Which test detects a reducing sugar?
questions.exp: Benedict's reagent turns from blue to brick-red in the presence of a reducing sugar when heated.

questions.q: At which level of protein structure are disulfide bonds found?
questions.exp: Disulfide bonds (between cysteine –SH groups) contribute to the tertiary structure of proteins.

questions.q: What molecule is released in a condensation reaction?
questions.exp: Condensation reactions join monomers with the release of water.

questions.q: Why is glycogen more suitable than glucose for energy storage in animals?
opts: Glycogen is insoluble/compact and does not affect osmotic potential
Glycogen has more energy per gram
questions.exp: Glycogen is an insoluble compact polymer — it does not affect osmotic potential and stores large amounts of glucose in a small volume.
